overview.main_topic: The remaining steps for customizing fit() via train_step(), two important notes, and a complete TensorFlow implementation with a loss-tracking metric exposed through the metrics property.
overview.central_idea: A custom train_step() contains the same forward pass / GradientTape / optimizer.apply logic as a hand-written step, and returns a dict of metric values. Listing metric objects in the model's metrics property lets fit() reset them automatically each epoch and at the start of evaluate().
overview.importance: Listing 7.21 is the template for most custom training algorithms in Keras with TensorFlow: it shows the exact contract between your step and fit() (input data, returned logs, metrics property).

summary:
This page completes the recipe begun on p.246 for **customizing what `fit()` does**. After subclassing `keras.Model`, you (2) **override `train_step()`**, whose body is nearly identical to the training step functions written in section 7.4.2, and (3) **return a dictionary** mapping metric names, including the loss, to their current values.

Two notes follow. First, the pattern does **not** prevent you from using the Functional API: it works whether you build Sequential, Functional or subclassed models, because you only subclass `Model` to swap one method. Second, you **don't need `@tf.function` or `@jax.jit`** on your `train_step()`, since the framework compiles it for you.

Under the heading *Customizing fit() with TensorFlow*, **Listing 7.21** defines a module-level `loss_fn = keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy()` and `loss_tracker = keras.metrics.Mean(name="loss")`, then a `CustomModel` whose `train_step(self, data)` unpacks `inputs, targets`, runs `self(inputs, training=True)` inside a `tf.GradientTape`, computes the loss, takes `tape.gradient(loss, self.trainable_weights)`, applies them with `self.optimizer.apply(...)`, updates the loss tracker, and returns `{"loss": loss_tracker.result()}`. The callouts explain that `self(...)` is used instead of `model(...)` because the model is the class itself, and that listing `loss_tracker` in the **`metrics` property** makes the model call `reset_state()` on it at the start of each epoch and of each `evaluate()` call, so you don't reset by hand.

The final paragraph says that we can now instantiate, compile **with only an optimizer** (the loss is defined outside the model), and train with `fit()` as usual; the code for that is on p.248.

concepts.name: Overriding train_step()
concepts.definition: Subclassing keras.Model and redefining train_step(), which fit() calls per batch, to run a custom learning algorithm under fit().
concepts.intuition: fit() is the loop; train_step() is the loop body you are allowed to rewrite.
concepts.technical: train_step(self, data) unpacks the batch, computes predictions with self(inputs, training=True), computes a loss, gets gradients with the backend's mechanism, applies them with self.optimizer, updates metrics and returns a logs dict.
concepts.significance: Keeps callbacks, progress bars, compilation and distribution while allowing arbitrary per-batch logic.
concepts.misconception: That train_step() must be decorated with @tf.function; fit() compiles it for you.

concepts.name: The model.metrics property
concepts.definition: A property listing the metric objects the model owns; fit() and evaluate() call reset_state() on each of them at the start of every epoch and evaluation.
concepts.intuition: Registering your counters with the framework so it can zero them at the right moments.
concepts.technical: Overridden with @property def metrics(self): return [loss_tracker]. Any metric you want reset across epochs should be listed.
concepts.significance: Removes the manual reset_state() bookkeeping that a from-scratch loop requires (p.246).
concepts.example: Without it, the 'loss' shown in epoch 3 would be the average over epochs 1 to 3.
concepts.misconception: That metrics are reset automatically just because they are used in train_step(); they must be listed in metrics.

concepts.name: tf.GradientTape
concepts.definition: TensorFlow context manager that records operations so gradients can be computed afterwards with tape.gradient().
concepts.intuition: A recorder that watches the forward pass so it can replay it backward.
concepts.technical: Operations on watched variables inside the with-block are recorded; tape.gradient(loss, self.trainable_weights) returns a list of gradients, one per weight.
concepts.significance: The TensorFlow mechanism for the backward pass inside the custom train_step.
concepts.example: with tf.GradientTape() as tape: predictions = self(inputs, training=True)
concepts.misconception: That operations outside the with-block are recorded; the loss must be computed inside it.

concepts.name: Mean metric as loss tracker
concepts.definition: keras.metrics.Mean(name="loss") accumulates per-batch losses and reports their running average.
concepts.intuition: Smooths the noisy per-batch loss into an epoch-level average.
concepts.technical: update_state(loss) each batch; result() in the returned dict; reset by fit() because it is listed in metrics.
concepts.significance: Produces the same kind of 'loss' number the default fit() displays.
concepts.misconception: That the progress-bar loss is the current batch's loss; it is the average so far in the epoch.

code.title: Customizing fit(): TensorFlow version
code.original_code:
import keras
from keras import layers

loss_fn = keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy()
loss_tracker = keras.metrics.Mean(name="loss")

class CustomModel(keras.Model):
    def train_step(self, data):
        inputs, targets = data
        with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
            predictions = self(inputs, training=True)
            loss = loss_fn(targets, predictions)
        gradients = tape.gradient(loss, self.trainable_weights)
        self.optimizer.apply(gradients, self.trainable_weights)

        loss_tracker.update_state(loss)
        return {"loss": loss_tracker.result()}

    @property
    def metrics(self):
        return [loss_tracker]
code.what_it_does: Defines a Model subclass whose per-batch training logic is written by hand with TensorFlow's GradientTape, while still being driven by fit().

deeper.title: What fit() does around your train_step
deeper.body:
Beyond the book, a simplified picture of the outer loop:

1. At the start of each epoch, call `reset_state()` on every metric in `model.metrics`.
2. For each batch: call the (compiled) `train_step(batch)`, get the logs dict.
3. Pass the logs to callbacks (`on_train_batch_end`) and update the progress bar.
4. At epoch end, optionally run validation, call `on_epoch_end` callbacks, append logs to `History`.

Your override only replaces step 2's body; steps 1, 3 and 4 still happen.

deeper.title: Why the loss is defined outside the class
deeper.body: Listing 7.21 keeps `loss_fn` and `loss_tracker` as module-level globals for brevity. Beyond the book: a common alternative is to create them in `__init__` (e.g. `self.loss_tracker = keras.metrics.Mean(name="loss")`) so that several model instances don't share one tracker. With the global version, two `CustomModel` instances trained in the same session would update the same metric object.

misconceptions.correction: The pattern works with Sequential, Functional and subclassed models; p.248 passes a Functional graph to CustomModel(inputs, outputs).

misconceptions.correction: The framework compiles it for you.

misconceptions.claim: Metrics used in train_step() are automatically reset each epoch.

questions.question: What are the three steps for customizing fit() described across pp.246-247?
questions.answer: Subclass keras.Model; override train_step(); return a dictionary mapping metric names (including the loss) to their current values.
questions.explanation: The first bullet is on p.246, the other two at the top of p.247.

questions.question: Why does Listing 7.21 override the metrics property?
options: So that compile() can find the loss function
So the model automatically calls reset_state() on loss_tracker at the start of each epoch and of evaluate()
So that gradients are computed for the metric
So that the metric is saved with the model weights
questions.answer: So the model automatically calls reset_state() on loss_tracker at the start of each epoch and of evaluate()
questions.explanation: The callout states this purpose. The loss function is global, not a metric; metrics are not differentiated; saving is unrelated.

questions.question: Why does the listing call self(inputs, training=True) rather than model(inputs, training=True)?
questions.answer: Because train_step is a method of the model class itself; self is the model instance being trained, there is no separate model variable.
questions.explanation: Stated in the callout. training=True also ensures Dropout behaves in training mode.

questions.question: Why does compile() in this example receive only an optimizer?
options: Because Adam computes the loss internally
Because the loss is already defined outside the model and used directly in train_step()
Because Keras infers the loss from the output activation
Because losses are not allowed with subclassed models
questions.answer: Because the loss is already defined outside the model and used directly in train_step()
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says exactly this. Optimizers never compute losses; Keras does not infer losses from activations; subclassed models can use compiled losses.

questions.question: Do you need @tf.function on an overridden train_step()? What does this tell you about the trade-off between custom loops and fit()?
questions.answer: No; the framework compiles it for you. Staying inside fit() gives you performance optimizations for free, which you'd have to add yourself in a from-scratch loop.
questions.explanation: See the second note on p.247 and the list of fit() features on p.246.

questions.question: What would the 'loss' value reported in epoch 3 represent if the metrics property were removed?
questions.answer: The average loss over all batches of epochs 1, 2 and 3, because loss_tracker would never be reset.
questions.explanation: Without being listed, the tracker is not reset by fit(), so it keeps accumulating.

questions.question: Can you rewrite Listing 7.21 from memory and point out which lines would change for PyTorch?
questions.answer: The GradientTape block and tape.gradient call would be replaced by loss.backward() and reading v.value.grad, and the optimizer update wrapped in torch.no_grad() (p.248).
questions.explanation: Compare with p.248 to check yourself.
